One Net to Rule Them All.narr: Roboticists face a fundamental problem: a policy trained on one simulator learns to exploit that simulator's specific quirks—its exact friction coefficients, mass distributions, sensor calibrations. When deployed on a different platform, those learned shortcuts fail. This paper asks whether domain randomization can work across different robot bodies, not just within one. By randomizing not just physics but the fundamental kinematics and sensor modalities themselves, one policy can fly distinct quadcopters without retraining. The approach extends the randomization idea from a single sim's parameters to the entire problem space: if the policy generalizes across embodiments, real-world transfer becomes zero-shot.
One Net to Rule Them All.how:
The problem: A quadcopter policy learns motor constants, inertia tensors, and controller gains specific to its training platform. A different quad has different motor dynamics, so the learned policy either stalls or overshoots.

The mechanism: Instead of training on one quad's dynamics, randomize across a distribution of quad morphologies: vary motor constants (σ_motor), inertia scaling (σ_inertia), arm lengths, and sensor noise independently each episode. The policy must succeed not on any single quad but across all of them. Step by step: (1) Define parameter ranges for motor/inertia/geometry from manufacturer specs and empirical variance, (2) Each training episode draws new parameters, (3) Simulate and train the policy to generalize over that distribution, (4) At test time, a new quad's unknown parameters fall within the training range.

Why it works: The policy cannot memorize one quad's identity; it learns reliable control laws that work for any quad in the cloud. Real-world quads become just another sample from the trained distribution.

DrEureka.narr: Domain randomization requires humans to manually specify which parameters to randomize and how wide the ranges should be. Too narrow and the policy overfits; too wide and it becomes overly conservative. This paper sidesteps manual tuning by asking an LLM to design both the reward function and the randomization distribution. The LLM reads the task description, proposes ranges for friction, mass, and other parameters, and iteratively refines them based on sim-to-real gap feedback. The result: automatic curriculum and randomization ranges with no domain expert involved, often outperforming hand-tuned approaches.
DrEureka.how:
The problem: Humans must decide: randomize friction in [0.2, 1.0]? Or [0.5, 0.8]? There is no principled way, leading to tedious manual hyperparameter search.

The mechanism: An LLM loop: (1) The LLM reads the task ('pick a cube from a table') and generates a reward function R_proposed and parameter ranges [theta_min, theta_max], (2) Simulate training with these ranges for N episodes, measure sim success rate and estimated real success (via a simulator-to-real predictor), (3) Send feedback to the LLM: 'real success estimated at 34%; friction randomization may be too wide', (4) The LLM refines the ranges and reward, (5) Repeat until convergence. Key insight: the LLM proposes, the simulator verifies.

Why it works: The LLM uses common sense from training data (e.g., 'friction is usually 0.3-1.0 for robotics') and refines based on empirical feedback, automating what a human expert would do iteratively.

DemoStart.narr: Collecting demonstrations for dexterous manipulation is expensive—every failure can damage the hardware. DemoStart accelerates learning by starting with a small number of human-provided demonstrations, automatically building a curriculum from them, and applying domain randomization throughout. Rather than training from scratch on random initializations, the policy begins solving the task in configurations from the demos, gradually randomizing towards harder, unseen configurations. The combination of demo-led initialization and guided randomization achieves zero-shot dexterous transfer with far fewer real attempts.
DemoStart.how:
The problem: Dexterous tasks (in-hand object manipulation, tool use) need many demonstrations or long training. Asking for 1,000 human demos is impractical; asking the policy to learn from scratch via RL takes millions of sim steps.

The mechanism: (1) Collect K human demonstrations of the task (e.g., 20 dexterous grasps), each showing object initial pose and successful hand trajectory, (2) Extract task diversity from demos: the range of object sizes, poses, and hand start positions that appear, (3) Initialize policy training with imitation learning on these K demos (faster than RL from scratch), (4) Gradually randomize: epoch 1 demos from actual demo poses + 10% randomization, epoch 2 20% randomization, ..., epoch N full randomization across learned distribution, (5) Policy must succeed at both imitated poses and increasingly randomized variants.

Why it works: Demos provide a warm start and task-relevant distribution estimates. Gradual randomization lets the policy extend from what it knows (demos) to what it hasn't seen (randomized) without catastrophic forgetting.

Privileged-Dreamer.narr: A deployed policy never directly observes hidden parameters like the mass of the object it is grasping or the friction of the surface. Yet these parameters determine whether a grasp will slip, whether a push will succeed, or whether a throw will land. Privileged-Dreamer estimates these hidden parameters online during deployment by watching the robot's proprioceptive feedback—joint torques, accelerations, position errors—and conditioning the policy on the estimates. The policy acts as both controller and system identifier, inferring the environment's hidden state from its own proprioceptive stream.
Privileged-Dreamer.how:
The problem: A policy trained on [mass, friction] = [500g, 0.5] fails on [600g, 0.7] because the parameters changed. The camera does not directly see mass or friction—only the robot's motion and forces reveal them.

The mechanism: (1) During training in simulation, vary mass and friction randomly, (2) Record (joint positions q, velocities q-dot, torques tau, proprioceptive error residuals) as the policy executes, alongside ground-truth hidden parameters, (3) Train an estimation network E: (q, q-dot, tau history) → (mass_est, friction_est), in parallel with the policy, (4) Condition the policy on the estimated parameters: pi(action | image, estimated_mass, estimated_friction), (5) At deployment, the policy estimates parameters from live proprioception and adapts its behavior without human labels.

Why it works: Proprioceptive signals implicitly encode environment parameters. By learning to decode them, the policy becomes adaptive without requiring explicit system identification experiments.

Denoising World Model Learning.narr: Learned world models—networks that predict the next state from the current state and action—can replace hand-coded physics simulators. Yet they are notoriously brittle: small prediction errors compound over rollouts, diverging into unrealistic states. Denoising World Model Learning applies denoising diffusion techniques to world model training, explicitly modeling and reducing prediction uncertainty. The result is the first zero-shot humanoid transfer to outdoor terrain (snow, stairs) using only a learned dynamics model, showing that learned physics can match or beat hand-written simulators at generalization.
Denoising World Model Learning.how:
The problem: An MLP world model predicts delta-states: M(state, action) → next_state. But stochastic environments (soft ground, sensor noise) produce noisy targets. Standard MSE loss learns only the mean, ignoring uncertainty. Rollouts compound small errors into trajectories that diverge from reality within seconds.

The mechanism: (1) Add Gaussian noise to all state transitions during training: corrupted_next_state ~ N(actual_next_state, sigma^2 I), (2) Train the world model as a denoising network: M(state, action, noise_level) → predicted_next_state, predicting the mean and variance of the next state conditional on noise level, (3) Explicitly optimize a likelihood objective: minimize -log p(actual_next_state | state, action), which accounts for aleatoric uncertainty, (4) At rollout time, the model outputs distributions over states, and the policy can either sample or use the mean, (5) Crucially, the model learns to be uncertain in ambiguous situations, preventing overconfident divergence.

Why it works: By modeling epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, the learned dynamics avoids the compounding error problem. The model's uncertainty calibration lets policies that use learned models transfer better than those trained on point estimates.

World Models for General Surgical Graspi.narr: Surgical grasping requires precision: the gripper must approach the tissue without tearing it, apply just enough force, and retract smoothly. Real surgical data is scarce and expensive to collect. This work trains a learned world model on simulation with depth sensor uncertainty, then transfers the policy to real surgical tasks. The model learns not just forward dynamics but how depth sensors fail—occlusion, specularity, missing pixels—and the policy becomes reliable to these sensor quirks. The result: 69% real surgical success from a policy trained purely in simulation with a learned model, showing that uncertainty-aware learned physics can handle the gaps that hand-coded models miss.
World Models for General Surgical Graspi.how:
The problem: Surgical scenes are deformable, textureless, and have specular reflections that break depth cameras. A hand-coded physics model cannot capture soft tissue mechanics; a learned model trained on perfect simulation will overfit and fail on noisy real sensors.

The mechanism: (1) In simulation, add realistic depth sensor noise: missing pixels (occlusion behind tools), Gaussian depth noise (sigma=2mm), and drop 15% of the depth frame randomly to simulate specular failure, (2) Train a world model to predict the next state from noisy depth input: M(rgb+noisy_depth, action) → next_state, (3) The model learns to work despite incomplete and corrupted observations; it infers hidden state from available signals, (4) Augment training with domain randomization of tissue material properties (stiffness, damping) and tool geometry, (5) Transfer the learned model to real surgery: the policy has seen depth noise patterns in training, so real sensor artifacts are within distribution.

Why it works: Learned models can explicitly handle sensor uncertainty, unlike rigid-body simulators. Training with realistic sensor noise means the model transfers to real sensors that exhibit the same failure modes.

High-Density Visual Particle Dynamics.narr: Predicting dense particle dynamics (deformable objects, granular materials, fluids) is essential for manipulation but computationally expensive. Graph neural networks (GNNs) can learn dynamics but scale poorly: O(n^2) complexity for n particles. This paper proposes learning dynamics as high-density particle interactions using a sparse convolution approach, achieving 2x speedup over GNNs while maintaining quality. The learned model handles deformable bags, cloth, rope, and granular media, and policies trained on it transfer to real manipulation tasks. Speed and quality together make learned dynamics practical for real-time control.
High-Density Visual Particle Dynamics.how:
The problem: Deformable objects are common in manipulation but expensive to simulate. GNNs process all pairs of particles, scaling as O(n^2). For n=10,000 particles, this becomes prohibitive at control time (30 Hz requires <33 ms inference).

The mechanism: (1) Represent the object as a high-density particle cloud (implicit surface points), (2) For each particle, identify nearby particles within a radius (spatial hashing for O(1) lookup), (3) Use a sparse 3D convolutional network to aggregate interactions: ConvNet(particle positions + features, local_neighborhood) → local_forces, (4) Accumulate forces from neighbors and integrate: next_position = position + velocity*dt + force*dt^2/m, (5) Train on both simulated deformable objects and real video of manipulation to learn sim-to-real bridging.

Why it works: Sparse convolution exploits locality: particles only interact with neighbors, not all other particles. This reduces complexity and mimics how real physics works (local contact forces). The inductive bias allows learning accurate dynamics fast enough for closed-loop control.

World Model-Based Perception for Visual.narr: Training legged robots to walk from vision is hard: the robot must learn perception (what terrain is ahead), prediction (how the terrain will affect my motion), and control (which leg commands move safely). A teacher robot with proprioceptive feedback learns easily; a student robot with only vision struggles due to domain gap. This work uses a learned world model as a bridge: the model predicts the next visual frame given the current frame and action, and the policy learns to use this prediction to plan locomotion. The model acts as an implicit proprioceptive observer, teaching the policy to perceive terrain through its own predictive errors.
World Model-Based Perception for Visual.how:
The problem: A vision-only policy for legged locomotion must infer both static terrain (rocks, obstacles) and dynamic effects (ground compliance, friction) from images alone. The teacher policy with IMU + proprioception sees all of this directly and trains easily. The gap is huge: student trains 5x slower and converges to suboptimal control.

The mechanism: (1) The teacher policy outputs actions given [proprioceptive state, IMU, vision], (2) Train a world model in parallel: M(image_t, action_t) → image_t+1, learning to predict the visual consequences of actions, (3) The world model implicitly learns terrain properties: soft ground absorbs motion (different frame delta), rocks are rigid (larger frame shifts per action), (4) Give the student policy access to world model predictions: student_policy(image_t, predicted_image_t+1) → action, instead of just image_t, (5) The student uses prediction errors as implicit proprioceptive signals—when its actions don't match the prediction, it adjusts.

Why it works: The world model distills the teacher's proprioceptive knowledge into visual predictions. The student's policy learns by matching its actions to what the world predicts, closing the teacher-student gap without direct proprioceptive access.

Physically Embodied Gaussian Splatting.narr: Real2Sim requires capturing a scene and reconstructing it for simulation. Most reconstructions (NeRF, meshes) are optimized for rendering, not physics. This work proposes dual-representation Gaussian splatting: small particles for physics simulation (collisions, contacts) and 3D Gaussians for rendering (appearance). The particles are initialized from the Gaussian splat but optimized to match real object masses, friction, and restitution. Policies trained in this hybrid reconstructed sim transfer well to reality because the geometry matches precisely and the physics is calibrated. Marrying appearance reconstruction with physics calibration closes the Real2Sim gap.
Physically Embodied Gaussian Splatting.how:
The problem: A rendered scene (Gaussian splat or NeRF) looks photorealistic but contains no physics. Loading it into a physics engine requires guessing object masses, friction, and collision geometry—all sources of sim-to-real gap.

The mechanism: (1) Scan the real scene (photos from multiple angles) and fit a 3D Gaussian Splat (GS), learning position, opacity, color, and covariance of ~1M Gaussians, (2) Convert the Gaussian density into rigid-body collision shapes: for each object region identified in the GS, create a simplified mesh or capsule primitive, (3) Initialize particle masses and frictions from measured object properties (weigh the object, measure friction with a slider test), (4) Create two representations: (a) Gaussians for rendering (differentiable splatting during rollouts), (b) Particles+contact geometry for physics simulation, (5) Train RL policies in this hybrid sim; gravity and contacts are exact, appearance is photorealistic.

Why it works: Physics simulation requires shapes and parameters; rendering requires appearance. By decoupling, you get accuracy in both. Policies transfer because they learned on geometry and physics that exactly match reality, even though appearance was rendered.

Real-to-Sim Grasp.narr: When a grasp fails in reality, why? Did the gripper approach the wrong angle, or did the object slip due to miscalibrated friction? Real-to-Sim Grasp maps real observations back into clean simulation space to diagnose the gap. During a failed grasp, the method recovers the actual object pose, gripper pose, and estimated friction from the real scene, then replays that failure in simulation. This reveals which sim parameters caused the failure. By iteratively adjusting the sim to match observed failures, the simulator becomes a mirror of what is actually happening, and policies trained in it transfer.
Real-to-Sim Grasp.how:
The problem: A grasp policy fails on the real robot, but we don't know if the failure is due to wrong object detection, wrong gripper dynamics, or wrong friction. Training a new policy requires understanding the root cause.

The mechanism: (1) At failure time, use cameras + depth to recover real object 6D pose (via pose estimation network trained on sim data), real gripper geometry, and estimated contact points, (2) Measure or estimate real friction from the slip pattern: if the object slipped left after gripper closed, friction is below [calculated minimum], (3) Set up a simulation environment with the recovered poses, friction estimate, and object model, (4) Replay the gripper motion in sim and observe: does it fail in sim the same way? If yes, friction estimate is good. If no, adjust, (5) Collect 100+ failed grasps, tune friction/stiffness to match failure patterns, (6) Retrain policy with calibrated sim; transfer improves.

Why it works: Simulation parameters are not static; they depend on objects and conditions. By observing and inverting real failures, you recover the actual physical parameters, making the sim match reality for that specific scenario.

Learning Locomotion Affordances + Photor.narr: Humans demonstrate complex locomotion in videos: walking on different terrain, stairs, obstacles. Can videos of human motion teach a robot to walk? This work captures radiance fields from 10 hours of video of a human walking in varied environments, reconstructs a photoreal simulator from those fields, and trains a quadruped policy in it. The policy learns to navigate terrain types (grass, gravel, stairs) from visual affordances inferred from the video. The result: human locomotion video becomes training data for robots, without explicit motion capture or manual labeling.
Learning Locomotion Affordances + Photor.how:
The problem: Quadruped locomotion requires seeing terrain ahead. Simulation provides clean terrain but lacks perceptual realism. Real robot videos are sparse and hard to label. How do you get rich training data that shows both terrain and successful locomotion?

The mechanism: (1) Collect 10 hours of first-person video of a human walking outdoors, across grass, gravel, stairs, etc., capturing both locomotion and the visual context, (2) Fit a radiance field (NeRF-style) to the video, reconstructing a 3D scene with texture and lighting. The NeRF is trained only on the video frames and camera poses (estimated via SLAM), (3) Extract locomotion affordances: human footstep positions and timing from the video (via 2D pose estimation or inertial tracking), map to locations in the reconstructed 3D scene, (4) Use the radiance field as a camera source for sim: render virtual views from arbitrary positions in the reconstructed environment, (5) Train a quadruped policy: image_input → next_step_position, using rendered images from the radiance field. The policy sees both the affordances (where humans stepped) and the visual terrain (from the field's rendering).

Why it works: Radiance fields compress video into a 3D representation that can be rendered from new viewpoints, creating unlimited training data. Human affordances are implicitly encoded in the reconstructed geometry, so the policy learns from human expertise without explicit labels.

PhysX-Anything.narr: Creating a 3D simulation-ready asset from a single image is a holy grail for robotics: imagine showing a robot a picture of a new object and it instantly knows how to grasp, push, or manipulate it. PhysX-Anything takes a single image and reconstructs a physics-ready 3D asset: mesh geometry, estimated mass distribution, material properties, and collision shapes. The method uses a 2D diffusion model to hallucinate 3D geometry, and a learned predictor to estimate physics parameters from appearance. Grasping policies trained on the reconstructed objects transfer to real grasps. One image → simulation-ready object → real robot success.
PhysX-Anything.how:
The problem: Given an image of a mug, how do you build a 3D model for simulation? Manual modeling takes hours. Photogrammetry requires many angles. Can a single image suffice?

The mechanism: (1) A conditional diffusion model generates plausible 3D geometries (as point clouds or meshes) conditioned on the input image, trained on a large synthetic dataset of [image, 3D object] pairs, (2) Multiple samples are drawn and filtered: keep 3D reconstructions that when re-rendered match the input image (rendering loss as a filter), (3) Estimate physics parameters: a learned network predicts mass, center-of-mass, friction, and restitution from image appearance (e.g., metal is heavier and less deformable than plastic; smooth surfaces are more slippery), (4) Output a USD/URDF file with mesh, inertia tensor, and material properties, importable directly into a physics engine, (5) Train grasping policy on synthetic objects generated this way; test on real objects in the reconstructed sim.

Why it works: The diffusion model has seen many objects in training and learned plausible 3D geometry priors. The physics predictor uses visual cues (material appearance) to estimate properties. Together, a single image becomes a reasonable 3D-physics-ready asset without manual effort.

TieBot.narr: Tying a knot is a complex deformable-object manipulation task. It is easy for a human to learn from watching a video but hard for a robot to learn. TieBot proposes a closed-loop Real-to-Sim-to-Real learning process: a human ties a knot on video, the video is converted into a simulated trajectory (via 3D pose estimation), a policy is trained in sim, deployed on the real robot, and failure cases are fed back to improve the sim. The method iterates, refining both the simulator and the policy without requiring explicit kinesthetic teaching. The result: the robot learns to tie a knot from video, through simulation, and back to reality, closing a complete feedback loop from observation to action.
TieBot.how:
The problem: A rope is a flexible object with infinite degrees of freedom. It cannot be simulated perfectly, and learning directly from video is ambiguous (2D video contains no depth). How can a robot learn complex rope manipulation from human videos?

The mechanism: (1) Video of human tying a knot is processed: extract 3D poses of hands and rope from multi-camera views or monocular pose estimation (with depth cues), (2) Reconstruct the 3D knot-tying trajectory: hand poses, gripper state, rope shape sequence, (3) Solve inverse kinematics to convert hand trajectories to robot arm joint commands, (4) Train a policy in sim: state = (image_of_rope, pose) → action = (gripper_delta, force), using differentiable rope simulation (position-based dynamics or learned model), (5) Deploy on real robot. When it fails (e.g., rope slips), record the failure, re-estimate actual rope state from the real cameras, update sim parameters (rope stiffness, friction), retrain, (6) Iterate: each failure teaches the simulator something new.

Why it works: The sim acts as a learned bridge between video observation and robot action. Real failures refine the sim, making it more accurate. The policy benefits from both human knowledge (from video) and robot self-correction (from failures).

Manipulate-Anything.narr: Collecting demonstration data for manipulation tasks is expensive: each demo requires a human operator on real hardware. Manipulate-Anything uses a large multimodal language model (VLM) to generate zero-shot manipulation trajectories directly from task descriptions. A VLM already knows what 'pick up a cube' and 'push a button' mean, so it can predict plausible motion trajectories without seeing real examples. A policy then learns from these generated demonstrations. The result: imitation learning from synthetic VLM-generated data beats learning from real human data, showing that foundation-model knowledge can substitute for real demonstration collection.
Manipulate-Anything.how:
The problem: Behavioral cloning needs many (state → action) pairs. Collecting these pairs means running the robot and having a human operate it or teleoperate. This is slow and expensive. Can you skip collection and generate synthetic demos?

The mechanism: (1) A vision-language model (e.g., GPT-4V, Qwen) is prompted: 'The task is [pick a red cube]. The gripper is at [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]. The cube is at [0.4, 0.5, 0.1]. Generate the next 5 arm movements as a sequence of (dx, dy, dz, gripper_state).' The VLM outputs a plausible trajectory, (2) Render each predicted pose in simulation, capture images and actions: (observation_image, action) pairs, (3) Sample 50–100 variations: different cube positions, gripper initializations, task descriptions, to generate a synthetic dataset, (4) Train a behavioral cloning policy on these synthetic (image, action) pairs with standard supervised learning, (5) Deploy. The policy has learned to predict actions from images by imitating VLM-generated trajectories.

Why it works: The VLM already understands manipulation from its pretraining on internet text and images. When prompted with task and state, it outputs actions that are plausible (hand anatomy, object physics) and well-distributed (not stuck in obvious failures). The policy learns from this implicit knowledge encoded in the VLM.

GenSim2.narr: Large-scale task learning requires diverse demonstrations. Collecting 100+ different manipulation tasks with human teleoperation is impractical. GenSim2 asks: can language models write task curricula? An LLM generates descriptions of 100+ articulated manipulation tasks (pick, stack, arrange, push, pull, rotate), along with reward functions and initial object configurations. A policy is trained on the union of these LLM-generated task specs, learning a general manipulation skill. The result: training on LLM-written curricula gives 20% higher real-world success than training on a small set of human-collected tasks, showing that language models can design diverse task distributions that improve generalization.
GenSim2.how:
The problem: A policy trained on one task (pick red cube) fails on new tasks (pick blue cube, stack cubes). Training on many tasks requires collecting many demonstrations. Can you generate tasks without collecting new data for each?

The mechanism: (1) An LLM is prompted: 'Generate 100 manipulation task descriptions for a robot arm. Each task should specify: [object_1, object_2, ...], [goal_state], [reward_function].' The LLM outputs: Task 1: Pick blue cylinder and place in red bowl. Reward = 1 if object_center within 0.05m of bowl center, else 0. Task 2: Stack three blocks in order of height, etc., (2) For each task, a RL algorithm (PPO or similar) trains a single policy conditioned on a task embedding or language instruction, (3) The task descriptions from the LLM are diverse: they cover different object combinations, geometries, and goal configurations, (4) The policy learns a common representation across all tasks: image + task_description → action, generalizing to new tasks and real-world variations, (5) Deploy the multimodal policy with a language goal; it adapts.

Why it works: LLMs have seen diverse manipulation tasks in training data and can generate plausible new tasks. This distribution of tasks, though synthetic, teaches the policy richer representations than any single human-collected task can. The diversity acts as implicit data augmentation.

DexGraspNet 2.0.narr: Learning to grasp diverse objects requires grasp data. Collecting real grasp data is expensive; generating synthetic grasps in simulation is fast but usually fails on reality. DexGraspNet 2.0 generates 3.5 million synthetic grasps in simulation, carefully filtered and augmented to minimize the sim-to-real gap. The policy trained on these synthetic grasps achieves 91% success on diverse real objects, zero-shot. The success comes from three insights: (1) massive scale overwhelms sim errors, (2) filtering removes obviously bad grasps, (3) augmentation makes the policy reliable to visual domain shift. This is the current state-of-the-art in zero-shot sim-to-real grasping.
DexGraspNet 2.0.how:
The problem: Synthetic grasps suffer from sim-to-real gap: the gripper dynamics, object properties, and camera models in sim differ from reality. A policy trained on 100k synthetic grasps often fails 50% of the time on real objects. How do you scale sim-to-real grasping to 91% success?

The mechanism: (1) For each object in a large synthetic dataset (10k+ CAD models), sample 100–1000 random gripper poses around it, test each in simulation (does it lift the object without dropping?), retain successful grasps, (2) Augment object properties: randomize mass, friction, restitution, size ±20%, to create 3.5M grasp variations, (3) Filter grasps: discard those with high sensitivity to small perturbations (perturb object mass by 5%, recompute success; keep only reliable grasps), (4) For each grasp, record (object_image, gripper_position, gripper_orientation) and label success/failure, (5) Train a CNN to predict grasp success: image → logits for 50k candidate gripper poses per object, (6) At test time, for a real object: estimate its identity (via CLIP or detection model), sample candidate grasps for that object class, rank by predicted success, execute the top grasp.

Why it works: Scale and filtering go hand-in-hand. With 3.5M examples, the policy sees all variations of grasping mechanics. Filtering removes grasps that are brittle to uncertainty, leaving only those reliable to sim-to-real transfer. Augmentation during training ensures the policy handles the exact variability it will see on real objects.

Video2Robo.narr: Collecting robot training data requires staging scenes, placing objects, and recording demonstrations—slow and expensive. A single human video contains rich information: hand poses, object motions, scene structure. Video2Robo extracts robot trajectories directly from a human video using 3D Gaussian Splatting to reconstruct the scene, then renders unlimited photoreal training viewpoints of the reconstructed scene. The same 3D representation serves both perception (seeing the scene) and data generation (rendering training examples).
Video2Robo.how: The process: Film a human performing the task (e.g., picking an object) from one or more camera angles. Reconstruct the 3D scene as a Gaussian splat. Extract hand/object trajectories from the video via pose estimation. Re-render the trajectories from robot camera viewpoints using the splat. Vary object poses, lighting, and camera angles during rendering to create diverse training data. Why it works: The Gaussian splat preserves the scene's real appearance and geometry from the human video, so robot rendering inherits that realism. Extracting trajectories from human motion is easier than programming robot policies, and the splat can render any viewpoint, multiplying one video into thousands of training examples.

Synthetic Object Compositions.narr: Training reliable detection models requires diverse images with varied objects, backgrounds, and contexts. Synthetic images from renderers are too clean; real images are expensive to label. Synthetic Object Compositions proposes a middle ground: render individual objects in isolation with varied lighting, then algorithmically compose them into images with realistic backgrounds and occlusions. This creates 20 million composite synthetic images with automatic segmentation masks. Vision models trained on these compositions generalize to detection and grounding tasks on real images, outperforming models trained on hand-labeled real data at a fraction of the cost. Procedural composition amplifies object diversity without the manual annotation burden.
Synthetic Object Compositions.how:
The problem: Collecting labeled images (object boxes, segmentation masks) is expensive: $1–10 per image, weeks of annotation time. Synthetic rendering is fast but produces obviously fake images. Real images are needed for reliable detection.

The mechanism: (1) Render 10k objects individually (CAD models or photogrammetry scans) under varied lighting (5–10 HDR environments per object), yielding 50k–100k isolated object images with perfect masks, (2) Collect background images: internet photos, website screenshots, natural scenes, (3) Procedurally compose: for each target scene size (640×480), randomly select 3–8 background images, blend them (weighted sum), (4) Randomly select and place 1–5 objects: sample object images + masks, resize (50–200%), randomly rotate and translate, composite over background using mask alpha-blending, (5) Adjust lighting/color to match background: apply color transfer or histogram matching to make object colors consistent with background tone, (6) Output: composite image + per-object segmentation mask (free from rendering) + bounding boxes, (7) Train a YOLO or Mask R-CNN detector on millions of these procedurally-generated images.

Why it works: Procedural composition is fast (1000 images/minute) and produces diverse, labeled data automatically. By compositing onto real backgrounds and varying object sizes/poses, the synthetic data covers the distribution of real images better than hand-rendered scenes. The model sees realistic clutter and occlusion during training.

Mobile ALOHA.narr: Mobile manipulation—moving an object while navigating—is hard to learn because every failure requires human intervention to reset the system. Mobile ALOHA reduces the cost of data collection by designing a low-cost, low-inertia teleop interface: two smartphone-mounted arms. A human operator can remotely control the robot arm, collect data efficiently, and reset easily without stopping. A mobile manipulation policy trained on just 50 demonstrations collected via this interface can perform complex tasks like opening doors and picking objects in navigation contexts. The result: cheap hardware + good teleoperation design = complex skills from minimal demos.
Mobile ALOHA.how:
The problem: Mobile manipulation requires both arm and base control. Collecting data traditionally means: human at robot, teaches arm, resets, repeats. Reset time dominates, making data collection slow. Scaling to 1000 demos takes weeks.

The mechanism: (1) Design a cheap, handheld teleop interface: two lightweight robot arms with cameras mounted on smartphones, no need for the full robot to be present during teleoperation, (2) A human operator wears the two phone-arms and performs the task (navigate to a door, open it, walk to an object, pick it), (3) Record joint angles, gripper state, and camera streams from the phone-arms, (4) Process the data: invert kinematics to convert phone-arm poses to mobile manipulator joint commands (the kinematics differ, but the task trajectory is the same), (5) Train a policy: image (from robot camera) → (base velocity, arm joints, gripper), using behavioral cloning on recorded trajectories, (6) With 50 demonstrations collected efficiently (5 min per demo including reset), train a policy to 80%+ success on real tasks. Contrast: traditional teleoperation on the actual robot takes 1 hour per demo due to reset logistics.

Why it works: The teleop interface mimics the task; the policy learns to execute similar motions on its different morphology. Because reset is cheap (just put the phones down, no robot reset needed), human can focus on task execution, not logistics. 50 high-quality task demos beat 1000 low-quality demos with poor reset handling.

Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI).narr: Teleoperation systems are expensive and require custom hardware. Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) proposes a different approach: use a hand-held gripper (low-cost, ~$500) to demonstrate manipulation tasks without a robot. The human holds the gripper, moves it naturally, and records end-effector poses. These human-collected gripper trajectories become training data for a robot arm, which must learn to execute similar motion patterns. The result: complex manipulation skills from human data collected with zero specialized equipment, and the skills transfer to unseen robot morphologies. Human embodiment is the teleoperation interface.
Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI).how:
The problem: Teleoperation rigs (haptic arms, VR gloves) are expensive and require setup time. Can you collect manipulation data with minimal hardware?

The mechanism: (1) A person holds a hand-held gripper (tracked via IMU or external camera), performs manipulation tasks: picking up objects, placing them, tool use, ~50 demonstrations of various tasks, (2) For each demo, record: gripper pose (6D: position + rotation), gripper state (open/closed/pinch), force/torque if available, (3) Extract task-agnostic features: gripper trajectory in end-effector space, relative object motion, interaction timing, (4) Train a policy on a robot: image (from robot camera) + language_goal → arm_joint_deltas, using BC on human gripper trajectories mapped to robot kinematics (via IK), (5) The policy learns end-effector motion patterns from human demonstrations without ever seeing a robot during data collection, (6) Deploy: the policy outputs end-effector targets, an IK solver converts to robot-specific joint commands.

Why it works: The human is the teleoperator; the gripper is just a pose sensor. This decouples demonstration from the robot, making data collection cheap and morphology-agnostic. End-effector trajectories transfer across different robot arms (7-DOF, 6-DOF) because the task is defined in end-effector space, not joint space.

HumanPlus.narr: Humanoid robots can imitate humans: watch a person move, extract their pose, and command the robot to adopt similar poses. HumanPlus goes further: 40 hours of human motion capture from in-the-wild video (not mocap suits, just RGB video) teaches a humanoid to shadow the human's movements with high fidelity. The policy learns a human motion representation and adapts it to the robot's body. Then, through reinforcement learning, the robot learns to accomplish tasks (walking, picking up objects) while maintaining humanoid naturalness. The result: embodied foundation models trained on human video, then fine-tuned for task control.
HumanPlus.how:
The problem: Humanoid robots are expensive to teleoperate, and data collection is slow. But humans move naturally and could serve as demonstrations—if we can extract and transfer their motions.

The mechanism: (1) Process 40 hours of in-the-wild human video: extract 3D poses using a pose estimator (MediaPipe 3D, or learned model), frame-by-frame, (2) Represent each pose as a skeleton vector: joint positions in body-frame coordinates (frame-agnostic), (3) Train a motion encoder: a transformer that maps sequences of human poses → latent codes, learning a compressed representation of natural human motion, (4) Train a policy to shadow humans: given human pose, output robot joint commands to minimize pose difference, using BC on extracted human poses, (5) Fine-tune with RL: the policy is initialized with human-imitation behavior, then trained with task rewards (move forward, pick up object), so the robot learns tasks while staying close to human motion patterns.

Why it works: Humans have solved the problem of natural, balanced movement. By extracting and imitating human motion, the robot starts with a reasonable prior (good balance, natural gait). Task RL then refines this prior for specific objectives. The result is a humanoid that moves naturally and can accomplish tasks—an embodied foundation model.

Open-TeleVision.narr: Teleoperation over the internet offers access to shared robot fleets and expert operators. But latency (even low-latency networks have 50–100 ms delay) breaks immersion and makes fine control difficult. Open-TeleVision adds immersive stereo teleoperation: the remote operator wears an AR/VR headset with dual cameras (stereoscopic), and the robot arm wears corresponding cameras on its wrist. The operator sees a live 3D view from the robot's perspective and controls the arm naturally. This sense of presence dramatically improves data quality: operators can collect complex trajectories (manipulation, precise placement) from remote locations. The data is high-fidelity enough that policies trained on it transfer well to real tasks. Immersion + stereo = high-quality remote teleoperation data.
Open-TeleVision.how:
The problem: Remote teleoperation has latency (network + processing ~100–200 ms). Without visual immersion, operators struggle with depth and fine control, leading to many failed/poor demonstrations. Collecting 1000 high-quality demos is slow.

The mechanism: (1) The robot arm wears stereo cameras (two cameras ~6.5 cm apart, mimicking human eye separation) on or near the wrist, transmitting video to the operator's headset at 60 Hz, (2) The operator wears an AR/VR headset (Meta Quest, HoloLens) with built-in headtracking and hand-tracking, (3) The headset displays the stereo robot-camera feed in real-time (accounting for known latency), creating a 3D perspective, (4) Hand-tracking translates operator hand motion into arm joint commands (via IK or learned policy), gripper commands from pinch gestures, (5) Tactile feedback (optional): haptic gloves or controllers convey robot gripper force, closing the loop, (6) The operator guides the arm to pick, place, manipulate objects, with stereo vision enabling precise depth estimation (no guesswork), (7) Record joint angles, gripper state, and camera streams from all demonstrations.

Why it works: Stereoscopic vision provides depth cues that monocular video cannot. With immersion (headtracking, hand-tracking), the operator is cognitively present in the robot's workspace. This improves demo quality: fewer collisions, more precise placements, natural motion. High-quality demos mean policies train faster and transfer better.

Scaling Cross-Embodied Learning (CrossFo.narr: CrossFormer trains one policy on trajectories from 20 different robot morphologies (arms, wheeled bases, quadrupeds), each contributing trajectories to a shared 900k-example dataset. Instead of separate models per robot, it learns a single, morphology-agnostic representation that captures the task—where to reach, how to grasp—while ignoring which body is executing the motion.
Scaling Cross-Embodied Learning (CrossFo.how: The policy encodes observations and language goals into a body-agnostic feature space via a transformer backbone. Each morphology has its own action head that maps shared features to its unique kinematics. During training, the shared encoder and task-specific heads are optimized jointly across all embodiments, so gradients from diverse robots reinforce common understanding of the task.

One Policy to Run Them All.narr: Instead of collecting separate data for legged robots (humanoids, quadrupeds, bipeds), this work shows that a single policy can zero-shot transfer across body shapes by extracting task-level commands that are independent of morphology. The encoder learns what 'walk forward' or 'turn left' means without reference to joint counts or limb lengths.
One Policy to Run Them All.how:
1. Encode observations and goals into task-level intent (a direction, a target state, a primitive action) that any legged body can understand.
  2. Each embodiment has a local policy head that converts task intent to its own joint actions, tuned on a small amount of in-distribution data.
  3. At test time, swap morphology-specific heads while reusing the shared task encoder, achieving zero-shot generalization.

Octo.narr: Octo is a generalist policy pretrained on 800k trajectories from the Open X-Embodiment dataset, spanning 22 different robot embodiments and diverse tasks (pick, place, push, primitive skills). It learns a universal feature space for robot behavior that can adapt to any morphology or task with minimal fine-tuning.
Octo.how:
1. Train a transformer-based policy on the union of all embodiment data, where embodiment identity is passed as a conditioning input.
  2. The policy learns to predict actions given observations, language goals, and embodiment context, absorbing common patterns across tasks and bodies.
  3. At deployment, the pretrained backbone plus a small task-specific head (trained on a few target examples) achieves strong performance, drawing on the broad prior.

RoboWheel.narr: RoboWheel scales cross-embodiment learning by automatically extracting and normalizing demonstrations from human operators teloperating different robots. It learns to map human motion (captured from mocap or hand tracking) into robot actions that generalize across embodiments, pooling human supervision across many platforms.
RoboWheel.how:
1. Record human teleoperation trajectories (hand poses, body motion) from one or more human teachers across multiple robot platforms.
  2. Learn a mapping from human-space demonstrations to robot-agnostic action representations, decoupling the human's intention from the specific robot they pilot.
  3. Any new robot can adopt the learned human-to-action mapping, instantly acquiring a policy from the pooled human data without requiring direct teleoperation on that platform.

TRANSIC.narr: TRANSIC corrects sim-trained policies by accepting human feedback in real time: the human operator watches the robot attempt a task and signals when and where the policy makes mistakes, and the residual network learns to predict the needed correction from that feedback without requiring a full policy retrain.
TRANSIC.how:
1. Start with a frozen sim-trained policy that does 90% of the task but fails in specific ways (wrong timing, wrong approach angle).
  2. A human operator provides corrections (either as target pose nudges or as success/failure signals) on a small number of real trials.
  3. A lightweight residual network learns to predict corrections conditioned on visual observations and the base policy's decision, minimizing the need for real-world data while accommodating multiple failure modes.

From Imitation to Refinement.narr: A base policy trained in simulation reaches the target location but is too coarse for tight-tolerance tasks like peg-in-hole insertion. This work trains a residual policy with RL, using only the base policy's approximate behavior as an initializer and a small real dataset to refine the last millimeters of precision.
From Imitation to Refinement.how: Freeze the sim-trained base policy and add a small learnable residual network that outputs small corrections to joint positions. Use RL (with a reward for successful insertion or contact) to optimize the residual on real robot trajectories, so the policy learns to read visual cues of misalignment and adjust in-flight. The base policy provides a good starting behavior, so the residual only needs to learn the fine details.

RL2AC.narr: RL2AC combines a fixed feedforward policy (trained in sim) with a real-time adaptive controller that runs at 1 kHz to reject disturbances the policy did not anticipate. When the real robot encounters friction shifts, vibrations, or model errors, the adaptive control layer compensates without retraining the policy.
RL2AC.how:
1. Deploy a sim-trained policy that outputs nominal actions without any adaptation.
  2. At runtime, an adaptive controller (using proprioceptive feedback—joint angles, forces—and a learned error model) generates small corrections to track the policy's intended trajectory in the face of unmodeled dynamics.
  3. The high-frequency (1 kHz) adaptation loop runs asynchronously from the policy network, allowing physics-based compensation without policy retraining.

Bridging the Sim-to-Real Gap via Informa.narr: This work identifies that sim-trained policies often memorize simulator artifacts (textures, exact physics constants, sensor noise signatures). An information bottleneck learns which features of the observation are truly predictive of success and which are simulator-specific, then distills these task-relevant features into a more transferable policy.
Bridging the Sim-to-Real Gap via Informa.how: Train the policy with an information bottleneck layer that compresses observations into a limited-dimensional feature vector. Supervise which features are 'task-critical' using labels from real data or privileged information (e.g., an oracle indicating which parts of the image matter). At deployment, the compressed representation throws away simulator artifacts, and the policy trained on these privileged features transfers better to reality than one trained on raw observations.

Automated Creation of Digital Cousins.narr: Instead of trying to match every detail of the real robot (geometry, physics properties, sensor calibration), digital cousins preserve the most task-relevant features—geometry and semantic meaning—while relaxing pixel-perfect accuracy. The approach automatically reconstructs these 'cousins' from brief videos or images, creating digital replicas optimized for sim training, not photorealism.
Automated Creation of Digital Cousins.how:
1. Capture video or images of the target robot and environment from multiple viewpoints.
  2. Reconstruct geometry (as a mesh or Gaussian splat) and infer high-level semantic properties (which surfaces are rigid, which are graspable) without hand-tuning physics constants.
  3. Load the reconstructed geometry and semantics into a simulator, optionally with learned or approximate dynamics, and train policies in the replica. The match to real geometry is sufficient; pixel-perfect appearance is not required.

URDFormer.narr: URDFormer infers the full URDF (Unified Robot Description Format) simulation file—kinematics, dynamics, joint limits—directly from a single image of a robot in a natural pose. It learns to 'see' the structure and parameters a simulator needs by training on images paired with known robot URDFs, then transfers to unseen robots or configurations.
URDFormer.how:
1. Train a transformer-based model on image-URDF pairs, learning to predict joint structure, link masses, and kinematic chain from visual appearance.
  2. At inference, take a single image of an unknown robot, and the model outputs an estimated URDF that can be loaded into simulation.
  3. Policies trained in the inferred simulator transfer better than those trained in generic hand-authored models, because the structure and parameters are tuned to the visible robot.

Learning Object Properties via Different.narr: Instead of measuring object properties (mass, friction, elasticity) by hand before simulation, this work learns them from proprioceptive data (joint torques, accelerations) recorded during the robot's interaction with the object. A differentiable simulator is optimized to match the observed proprioceptive traces, inferring properties that make the real-world data consistent.
Learning Object Properties via Different.how: Run excitation trajectories (pokes, pushes, lifts) on the real robot while recording proprioceptive signals. Optimize a simulator's object properties (mass, friction, contact stiffness) to minimize the mismatch between simulated and real proprioceptive outputs. The differentiable simulator acts as a loss function, and gradient descent tunes properties until the sim predictions match reality. These learned properties then improve transfer of policies trained in the sim.

Visual Forklift Zero-Shot Sim2Real.narr: A photoreal digital twin is reconstructed from real images of a warehouse scene, complete with geometry and appearance. A manipulation policy trained entirely in this faithful sim achieves strong zero-shot transfer on the real forklift task, because the visual distribution matches—the policy has seen the exact lighting, clutter, and objects it will encounter.
Visual Forklift Zero-Shot Sim2Real.how:
1. Scan or photograph the real warehouse and reconstruct it as a high-fidelity 3D asset (mesh with textures, lighting matched to reality).
  2. Place a simulated forklift and objects in the reconstructed warehouse and train a vision-based policy with sim-to-real domain randomization.
  3. Because the sim already shows real appearance, less randomization is needed, and the policy trains faster. Zero-shot transfer works because the real test environment is the same as the one the policy saw in training.

MatchMask.narr: When segmentation labels are scarce, MatchMask uses diffusion models to synthesize the missing training images. It generates variations by diffusing images while conditioning on a spatial mask (telling the model 'paint a new object here'), and these mask-conditional generations preserve label validity because the mask constrains where changes occur.
MatchMask.how:
1. Start with a small labeled segmentation dataset.
  2. For each labeled image, use a diffusion model to generate variations: condition the diffusion on a foreground/background mask, then sample new appearances for the masked region while keeping the background fixed.
  3. The generated images inherit correct labels from the original mask-conditional generation process, so no relabeling is needed. Train a segmentation model on the augmented dataset.

Role-SynthCLIP.narr: Role-SynthCLIP uses an MLLM (multimodal large language model) to generate diverse image-caption pairs for CLIP training by asking it to role-play: 'You are a dataset curator generating diverse robot images.' The role-play prompts guide the MLLM to produce richer, more varied synthetic training data than direct prompts would.
Role-SynthCLIP.how:
1. Prompt an MLLM with a role-play instruction: 'You are a dataset curator. Generate descriptions of robot images in different scenarios: picking, placing, reorienting. Vary: objects, lighting, camera angle, robot type, clutter.'
  2. The model generates diverse captions for hypothetical robot images, respecting the role context and scenario diversity.
  3. Use these captions (or generate images from them via another generative model) to create image-text pairs, then train CLIP on the synthetic pairs to learn vision-language alignment.

Ditto/Editto.narr: Ditto/Editto generates 1 million instruction-edit video triplets by combining a VLM (Vision-Language Model) with diffusion: given a seed video, the VLM writes an instruction (e.g., 'move object left'), and diffusion edits the video to show that instruction being executed. The result is a massive synthetic instruction-following dataset.
Ditto/Editto.how:
1. Start with a seed video showing a robot or human performing a task.
  2. Have a VLM describe the motion and propose an alternative instruction: 'The original video shows X. Edit it to show Y instead.'
  3. Use a video diffusion model to generate a new video where the action matches the alternative instruction, conditioned on the original.
  4. The VLM-generated instruction pairs with the diffusion-edited video to create (instruction, before-video, after-video) triplets. Train an instruction-following policy on these triplets.

OntoAug.narr: OntoAug keeps generative augmentation semantically valid by consulting an ontology: when diffusion generates a new image, the ontology constraints (e.g., 'if the object is a mug, the color must plausibly be mug-colored') are enforced. This prevents drift where synthetic images become visually incoherent or semantically implausible.
OntoAug.how: Define an ontology of task-relevant properties (object categories and their attributes: colors, sizes, materials that are realistic). When using diffusion to augment images, condition the diffusion on the ontology: 'Generate a new image with a red mug and a white table.' The diffusion model learns to respect these semantic constraints, preventing unrealistic augmentations that would teach the model false patterns. Train the perception model on ontology-constrained synthetic images.

Expert-Teacher-Student for Domain Adapti.narr: When adapting an object detector from synthetic to real data, this work enrolls foundation models (pre-trained experts on real-world visual understanding) as teachers. The detector learns from both the synthetic labels and the foundation models' predictions on real data, guiding adaptation toward real-world visual patterns without requiring manual annotations.
Expert-Teacher-Student for Domain Adapti.how:
1. Train a student detector on synthetic data with clean labels.
  2. At adaptation time, run the student on unlabeled real images and also query foundation-model experts (e.g., CLIP, SAM) for their predictions on the same images.
  3. Use the expert predictions as pseudo-labels and fine-tune the student with a mix of synthetic labels and expert pseudo-labels. The experts act as an external signal guiding the student toward real-world distributions.

VLM-Guided Source-Free Domain Adaptation.narr: A model trained on synthetic data is adapted to real images without accessing the original synthetic data or obtaining real labels. A VLM (vision-language model) scores real-image predictions, and optimal transport aligns the feature distributions of the student model to match the VLM's preferred feature space, adapting purely through feature alignment.
VLM-Guided Source-Free Domain Adaptation.how: Extract features from the student detector on real images. Query a VLM to score these predictions, identifying which real-image predictions the VLM finds plausible. Formulate adaptation as an optimal transport problem: find a feature transformation that aligns the student's real features with a VLM-guided reference distribution. Update the model to minimize this transport distance, effectively adapting the feature space without labels or access to training data.

UDAPose.narr: Pose estimation models trained on normal-light synthetic data fail under low-light conditions because the visual appearance shifts dramatically. UDAPose uses diffusion models to synthesize low-light variants of training images (darkening, adding noise, reducing contrast) and combines this with attention mechanisms that learn which image regions remain reliable in low light.
UDAPose.how:
1. Use a diffusion model conditioned on 'low light' to transform synthetic pose-training images into darker, noisier variants. The diffusion preserves keypoint locations (the labels) while changing appearance.
  2. Train the pose estimator on both normal and augmented low-light images, with an attention mechanism learning which features (e.g., sharp edges, high-contrast regions) are predictive in each lighting condition.
  3. At test time on real low-light scenes, the attention mechanism down-weights unreliable features and leans on low-light-adaptive ones.

GeCo-SRT.narr: GeCo-SRT (Geometry-aware Continual Sim-to-Real) adapts policies continuously as they deploy, using geometry-level consistency checks to detect when the sim has drifted from the real world. Instead of waiting for task failures, it proactively adapts the policy whenever geometric predictions (e.g., object positions) diverge from visual observations.
GeCo-SRT.how:
1. Maintain a geometric model of the scene (object poses, workspace layout) predicted by the policy's internal models.
  2. Compare predicted geometry to actual visual observations (via SLAM or other localization). When discrepancy exceeds a threshold, the policy's internal world model has drifted.
  3. Trigger continual adaptation: update the policy's feature representations or world model using the real observations as supervision, so the policy re-synchronizes without task failure.

Verifier-Guided Pseudo-Labeling for Poin.narr: Point tracking in robot workspaces requires precise bounding boxes for tracked objects, but human annotation is expensive and slow. Pseudo-labeling accelerates this by having a trained model predict boxes on unlabeled frames, but those predictions can be wrong. This family introduces a separate learned verifier network that scores each predicted label's reliability, filtering out low-confidence pseudo-labels before they corrupt the next training round. The verifier acts as a quality gate, allowing scale without collapse.
Verifier-Guided Pseudo-Labeling for Poin.how: The machinery: Train a teacher detector on hand-labeled data. Run it on unlabeled frames to produce candidate boxes with confidence scores. Train a verifier—a separate lightweight network—to predict whether each candidate box is correct by examining visual cues and the detector's output distribution. During retraining, keep only pseudo-labels the verifier approves (e.g., confidence > 0.85). Use the improved student as the next teacher, repeating the cycle. Why it works: The verifier learns to spot systematic failure modes (occlusions, blur, shadows) that the detector misses, breaking the error-accumulation loop that kills naive pseudo-labeling.

Topology-based Pseudo Labeling.narr: Pseudo-labels work when the unlabeled data distribution matches the training set, but robotics scenarios shift domains constantly: different lighting, camera angles, object appearances. A naive pseudo-labeled model overfits to the training domain and its errors multiply when the visual appearance changes. This work uses topological constraints on predicted labels—ensuring that spatial relationships and object orderings stay consistent—so pseudo-labels remain reliable even when appearance shifts.
Topology-based Pseudo Labeling.how: The key operation: Instead of filtering pseudo-labels by detector confidence alone, verify that predicted boxes maintain topological invariants: if object A was left of object B in the training set, it should stay left of B in unlabeled data (modulo natural rearrangements). Encode these constraints as a differentiable loss during retraining. Why topology helps: Spatial relationships are preserved across viewpoint and lighting changes where pixel-level features are not. A detector confused by new lighting still places objects in the right relative order, and topology-based filtering keeps those correct labels while rejecting ones that violate learned spatial patterns.

GaussianMatch.narr: Pseudo-labeling for regression tasks (e.g., predicting object poses, joint angles) is harder than classification because continuous outputs have infinite ways to be slightly wrong. A model trained on its own slightly-wrong predictions diverges quickly. GaussianMatch filters pseudo-labels for regression by requiring consistency across multiple views or frames of the same object: if three camera views agree on the object's 3D position via Gaussian splat reprojection, the pseudo-label is trustworthy; if they disagree, it is discarded.
GaussianMatch.how: The process: Fit a Gaussian splat to the scene from multi-view captures. Use the splat to reproject predicted object positions from multiple viewpoints. Compute the Gaussian match score: how well do the reprojected views align? Keep pseudo-labels with high match scores; discard outliers where views conflict. Train the regression model on the filtered pseudo-labels. Why it works: Multi-view consistency is a geometry-aware signal that does not require semantic labels. A model making small errors in pose will cause splat reprojections to disagree, automatically flagging those pseudo-labels as unreliable without any human judgment.

Scaling Robot Policy Learning via Zero-S.narr: Collecting labeled demonstrations across many robot platforms is prohibitively expensive: each arm, gripper, and locomotor type requires its own annotation effort. Zero-shot labeling sidesteps this by using a foundation model to auto-annotate diverse robot datasets without any task-specific training. A VLM like GPT-4V watches robot videos, understands the task semantics, and predicts object locations, grasp points, and success/failure labels directly, scaling labeling across embodiments at the cost of GPU inference.
Scaling Robot Policy Learning via Zero-S.how: The machinery: Collect unlabeled videos from many robot platforms (WidowX, Franka, Spot, etc.). Feed video frames to a foundation model with a prompt like "Where is the gripper attempting to grasp the object? Draw a bounding box." The model outputs zero-shot predictions. Filter predictions by the model's confidence and cross-frame consistency (adjacent frames should predict similar labels). Train separate embodiment-specific policies on the auto-labeled data. Why it works: Foundation models have learned rich semantics from internet-scale data and generalize across robot morphologies because they understand task goals (grasp, push, reach) abstractly, not morphology-specifically.

Learnability-Guided Diffusion for Datase.narr: Distilling a large dataset into a tiny synthetic one is hard: most selection methods pick representative examples, but a tiny set of typical configurations teaches a model less than a set of rare, hard, or complementary ones. This work uses a diffusion model guided by learnability scores to synthesize not the most representative examples but the most learnable ones—configurations that improve the gradient signal and reduce redundancy. The model generates synthetic trajectories that cover different error modes and edge cases.
Learnability-Guided Diffusion for Datase.how: The process: Train a diffusion model on the large dataset. Compute a learnability score for each real sample (e.g., via influence functions or gradient-based importance). Use the diffusion model to sample new synthetic examples, conditioning on these learnability scores so generation focuses on complementary, hard-to-learn configurations. Train the policy on the distilled synthetic set. Why it works: High-learnability samples are ones where the policy is currently failing or uncertain, so a small set of synthetic examples targeting those regions carries more training signal per sample than a representative subset would.

Orthogonal Gradient Matching.narr: Dataset distillation typically tries to match gradients—optimizing synthetic examples so their gradient matches the real dataset's gradient—but this can cause over-smoothing: all synthetic examples converge to similar configurations. Orthogonal gradient matching preserves diversity by only matching gradient directions, not magnitudes, using singular value decomposition to align the subspace spanned by gradients rather than the gradients themselves.
Orthogonal Gradient Matching.how: The machinery: Compute gradients from both the real dataset and the synthetic candidate set with respect to the model's loss. Perform SVD on both gradient matrices to extract the top-k principal directions. Optimize the synthetic examples so their gradient directions align with the real directions, but do not enforce magnitude matching. Why it works: Magnitude matching forces all synthetic examples to be similar to achieve the same overall gradient. Direction-only matching allows synthetic examples to point toward the same loss minima but from different starting configurations, preserving the diversity needed to cover the full behavior distribution without redundancy.

EVLF.narr: Large datasets carry both visual and language information (captions, task descriptions), but distilling a multimodal dataset into a tiny condensed set is harder than distilling images alone: you must preserve both visual features and semantic alignment. Early vision-language fusion synthesizes examples that capture the cross-modal signal at distillation time by jointly optimizing visual features and language embeddings together, not separately, so the condensed set remains aligned across modalities.
EVLF.how: The approach: Instead of distilling images and text independently, train a joint vision-language encoder on the large dataset. When creating synthetic examples, optimize both pixels and embeddings simultaneously to match the cross-modal gradient. Use contrastive loss between images and their captions as the distillation target. Why it works: Vision and language provide complementary signals: an image alone may not capture task semantics (is this a hard or easy grasp?), but a caption provides that context. Early fusion during distillation ensures the synthetic set carries both the visual patterns and semantic labels needed to train a multimodal policy.

Learning to Learn Weight Generation.narr: Dataset distillation requires iteratively training models on synthetic data, then computing gradients to optimize the synthetic examples—expensive and slow. An alternative approach sidesteps the inner loop: generate network weights directly conditioned on a tiny synthetic dataset, skipping the expensive gradient-based training loop entirely. A meta-network learns to map from distilled examples to high-quality initialized weights, compressing learning into a single forward pass.
Learning to Learn Weight Generation.how: The machinery: Train a meta-network on task families to learn the mapping: (synthetic data, architecture) → initialized weights that perform well. This inner meta-training is expensive but one-time. At deployment, given a small distilled dataset, the meta-network generates weights in milliseconds. Why it works: The meta-network learns implicit priors about which weight initializations are compatible with which data patterns. Instead of optimizing weights through SGD (which requires many examples to avoid overfitting), the meta-network combines the distilled set's signal with learned structure in a single step, trading expensive inner-loop training for a learned implicit prior.

GraspSplats.narr: Collecting grasp demonstrations is tedious: place an object, grasp it, record the gripper-to-object approach. Even a 60-second video of a single grasp contains rich geometric data. GraspSplats reconstructs a scene from a short video as a 3D Gaussian splat, then generates dense grasp data by querying the splat for gripper poses that avoid collision and reach the object from many angles. One 60-second capture yields thousands of usable grasp examples.
GraspSplats.how: The machinery: Capture 60 seconds of video orbiting an object, or let a robot arm move around it. Fit a 3D Gaussian splat to the frames. Use the splat's geometry to query safe gripper approach trajectories: for each query pose, raycast through the splat to check collisions, compute reach distance, and score grasp quality. Generate labeled grasp examples: (object image, gripper pose) → success/failure. Why it works: The splat provides dense 3D geometry learned directly from real images, so collision queries are accurate. Unlike hand-labeled grasps (which are sparse), splat-based generation covers continuous pose space, and every collision-free path in the splat is a valid grasp.

EmbodiedSplat.narr: A Gaussian splat captures geometric structure but not semantics: which pixels are the gripper, which are obstacles, which are the target object. Semantic 3D Gaussian Splatting adds semantic segmentation to each Gaussian, allowing open-vocabulary scene understanding. EmbodiedSplat learns this online during deployment, continuously updating splat semantics as the robot collects new views, turning the reconstructed scene into a live semantic map that feeds both perception and data synthesis.
EmbodiedSplat.how: The approach: During deployment, as the robot moves around, refine the Gaussian splat with new camera frames. For each frame, extract semantic features from a VLM and backproject them to the Gaussians. Update each Gaussian's semantic embedding. Query the enriched splat to generate training data: "render me 100 views where the gripper is segmented" or "show me the object from 50 viewpoints." Why it works: Online feed-forward updates keep the semantic map synchronized with the robot's understanding of the scene. The robot can then query its own semantic map for data, generating training examples for any object or region it names, without re-scanning or re-annotation.

DualSplat.narr: Training Gaussian splats typically requires dense per-pixel labels: every pixel labeled as sky, table, gripper, or object. Collecting such dense segmentation is expensive. DualSplat sidesteps dense labels by using pseudo-mask bootstrapping: fit a splat with no labels, use it to render views, predict masks on those views with a foundation model, backproject to improve the splat, and repeat. The splat learns semantics from rendered consistency, not manual labels.
DualSplat.how: The machinery: Initialize a splat on RGB images alone (no semantic labels). Render a batch of views. Run a VLM on each view to predict rough segmentations (e.g., "find the gripper"). These are pseudo-masks: noisy but signal-bearing. Use them as weak labels to update the splat's semantic embeddings. Re-render and repeat. Each iteration refines the masks via splat geometry and renderer consistency. Why it works: A VLM makes mistakes on a single frame, but the splat's geometry constrains which masks are physically consistent. If a mask says "gripper at (100, 50)" in one view but the splat geometry puts the gripper at (110, 60) when reprojected, the contradiction forces learning. Over iterations, the geometry and masks co-refine until both are consistent.

Scaling-Aware Data Selection for E2E Dri.narr: Driving datasets can be massive (millions of frames), but not all frames teach equally: some are simple highway cruising, others are hard edge cases (occlusions, weather, rare maneuvers). Scaling-aware selection balances dataset size against sample quality by finding the Pareto frontier between scale and individual sample utility—selecting more data only if the marginal samples are instructive enough to justify the training cost.
Scaling-Aware Data Selection for E2E Dri.how: The process: Compute a utility score for each frame: how much does removing this frame hurt the model's loss? (via influence functions or gradient magnitude). Sort frames by utility. Incrementally add frames to the training set, computing validation loss at each step. Identify the point where adding cheaper, lower-utility data hurts more than it helps. Why it works: A small set of high-quality hard examples teaches a richer policy than a huge set of easy ones, but too-small sets underfit. Scaling-aware selection finds the sweet spot where dataset size and sample difficulty are balanced, maximizing performance per training step.

Online Data Curation via Marginal Contri.narr: Dataset curation usually happens offline: score all data, select a subset, then train. But this misses online signals: early in training, a sample might be essential; later it becomes redundant. Marginal-contribution curation dynamically scores each sample's value during training by measuring how much removing it would hurt the current model's loss, dropping low-contribution samples and replacing them with new data. This adapts curation to the training trajectory.
Online Data Curation via Marginal Contri.how: The machinery: During training, periodically compute each sample's leave-one-out loss impact: train with the sample, train without it, measure the difference. Rank samples by marginal contribution. Remove the bottom 10% (lowest contribution). Fetch new samples from the unlabeled pool and retrain. Repeat. Why it works: Early training benefits from diverse, easy samples for gradient signal. Mid-training needs hard samples to refine boundaries. Late training is mostly fitting noise unless the sample is an important outlier. Marginal-contribution curation tracks this dynamic and keeps only the currently useful data, reducing dataset size without hurting performance.

Den-TP.narr: Trajectory prediction datasets are imbalanced: common scenarios (straight roads, gentle turns) have thousands of examples; rare ones (sharp lane changes, sudden stops) have few. A naive training procedure overfits to common cases and fails on rare ones. Density-balanced curation plus evaluation (Den-TP) identifies and oversamples underrepresented trajectory types, then evaluates on a density-stratified test set to measure performance fairly across all behavior modes.
Den-TP.how: The approach: Cluster trajectories by their curvature, acceleration, and intent (via embedding). Identify clusters with few samples. Reweight the training loss so rare clusters contribute equally to gradient steps despite their scarcity. During evaluation, ensure the test set maintains the same density distribution as training (or reports performance per density bin separately). Why it works: Simple reweighting helps, but performance on rare cases is only meaningful if the test set includes enough rare cases to reduce variance. Den-TP pairs curation with stratified evaluation, ensuring learned policies are actually reliable to the rare modes they were trained to handle.

Concept-Aware Batch Sampling.narr: Training data contains conceptual themes: certain object materials (metal vs. plastic), certain grasp styles (power vs. precision), certain lighting conditions. If a batch samples uniformly from the full dataset, it mixes all concepts, and the model must learn their boundaries in every step. Concept-aware sampling forms batches within concept boundaries, so the model can focus on one concept's interior before mixing. This reduces interference and accelerates learning per batch.
Concept-Aware Batch Sampling.how: The machinery: Cluster training data by one or more semantic concepts (material type, object class, lighting, task difficulty). During training, sample batches from one concept cluster at a time, staying within-concept for several steps before switching. Track concept progress (e.g., loss on metal grasps vs. plastic). Why it works: Mixing concepts in every batch forces the model to learn all decision boundaries simultaneously, causing interference. Concept-stratified batching lets the model master one concept's interior (e.g., "all ways to grasp metal"), then build on that foundation. This is akin to curriculum learning but driven by semantic structure, not difficulty.

Test-Time Perturbation Tuning.narr: A policy trained on fixed data may fail in a new environment with slightly different visual appearance or sensor noise. Retraining is expensive, and the new domain may have no labels. Test-time perturbation tuning adapts a frozen policy at deployment by using uncertainty-guided data augmentation: identify which input perturbations (brightness, blur, noise) cause the model's output to become uncertain, and adapt batch normalization statistics to handle those perturbations reliably.
Test-Time Perturbation Tuning.how: The process: At test time, sample many perturbed versions of the current frame (e.g., brightness ±10%, slight blur, sensor noise). Measure the model's output variance across perturbations—high variance means high uncertainty. Identify the perturbations that cause most uncertainty.
