Update batch normalization running statistics by exposing them to those hard perturbations. Over time, the model becomes reliable to the test domain's natural variations. Why it works: The model's uncertainty signals which aspects of the input are important. Adapting batch norm to handle those aspects directly (without retraining) is fast and requires no labels. Uncertainty guidance focuses adaptation on the perturbations that actually hurt performance in the test domain.

Neural Collapse in Test-Time Adaptation.narr: Test-time adaptation does not always help—sometimes it makes things worse, corrupting the learned feature space. This work explains when and why via neural collapse: a geometric phenomenon where feature representations of different classes converge or diverge during training. Neural collapse predicts whether test-time adaptation will improve or harm performance, enabling selective application of adaptation only when feature geometry is favorable.
Neural Collapse in Test-Time Adaptation.how: The machinery: During test-time adaptation, monitor the feature geometry: compute the Gram matrix of class-wise mean feature vectors and measure whether they converge toward a simplex (good collapse, features separate) or collapse to a single point (bad collapse, features fold). Predict model performance from these geometric statistics. If collapse is favorable, proceed with adaptation; if not, skip it to preserve learned structure. Why it works: Bad collapse happens when adaptation breaks the learned decision boundaries faster than it can relearn them. Monitoring geometry provides an early-warning signal. Neural collapse theory connects geometry to optimization dynamics, so measuring collapse predicts whether adaptation will help or hurt before fully committing to it.

STAR.narr: Vision-language models like CLIP are pretrained on broad internet data, but they may not understand domain-specific robotic tasks. Fine-tuning them on a new domain requires labels and retraining. STAR (Soft Text Adaptation with Ranking) adapts VLMs at test time by learning soft prompt embeddings—vector updates to the text encoder's input—that specialize the model for the target domain without any retraining or labels. The adaptive prompts remain soft (continuous vectors) rather than discrete words, avoiding the brittleness of hard-prompt optimization.
STAR.how: The approach: Initialize learnable soft prompt embeddings. At test time, forward unlabeled test images through the model with the soft prompts, measure prediction consistency or self-supervised loss, and update only the soft embeddings via gradient descent. The model's weights stay frozen. After a few gradient steps (1-10), the soft prompts specialize the model's text encoder to the new domain. Why it works: Soft prompts have continuous parameter space and are differentiable end-to-end, so gradient updates to them are stable. Because only the small prompt embeddings change (not the model), adaptation is fast and low-risk: if it hurts, reverting is instant.

CD-Buffer.narr: Detection models trained on clean data fail in adverse weather (rain, snow, fog) because appearance distributions shift sharply. Retraining is slow, and a deployed detector cannot wait. CD-Buffer (Concurrent-Dual Buffer) adapts at test time using a dual-buffer scheme: one buffer tracks the model's own predictions on test frames (a pseudo-label source), another tracks a reference distribution from clean data. The model adapts by balancing these buffers, staying anchored to learned knowledge while drifting toward the test domain. The dual-buffer balance prevents catastrophic forgetting.
CD-Buffer.how: The machinery: Maintain two buffers: one stores recent test detections (pseudo-labels), one stores reference detections from clean training data. Mix predictions from both buffers: output predictions are averaged weighted toward the buffer that predicts more confidently. Over time, retrain the model on the mixed buffer. Why it works: If the model adapted only to test pseudo-labels, error accumulation would corrupt it within hours. Dual-buffer mixing acts as a regularizer: the reference buffer keeps the model honest, preventing drift into wrong detections. The adaptive buffer lets the model shift gradually toward rain/fog/snow when those domains are consistent, but resists shifting if they are just noise.
